findings.claim: Hoisting `allowHeadersStr` out of the request handler can break the per-request fallback to the incoming `Access-Control-Request-Headers` header.
findings.rationale: In typical CORS middleware implementations (including Hono's), when `opts.allowHeaders` is empty the preflight response echoes the request's `Access-Control-Request-Headers` value, which is inherently per-request. Computing a single `allowHeadersStr` at middleware-construction time is only safe if the handler still keeps that dynamic branch; if the handler was refactored to just use `allowHeadersStr`, preflight responses will silently stop advertising the requested headers. I can't see the handler body in this hunk, so this is a suspicion worth verifying at the usage site.

findings.claim: Caching the joined header strings freezes the values, changing behavior if the caller mutates the arrays passed in `options` after `cors()` is called.
findings.rationale: Previously the `join(',')` presumably happened per request, so pushing to the array reference the caller supplied (e.g. `const headers = []; app.use(cors({ allowHeaders: headers })); headers.push('X-Foo')`) would be reflected. Now the strings are computed once at setup. Unusual but plausible usage; the change is silent. Moderate-low confidence anyone relies on it.

findings.claim: `?.length` collapses both "empty array" and "undefined" into `undefined`, losing the distinction of an explicitly empty allow/expose list.
findings.rationale: Defaults set `allowHeaders: []` / `exposeHeaders: []`, and a caller can also pass `{ exposeHeaders: undefined }` via the spread. With this change no `Access-Control-Expose-Headers` header is emitted for an empty list. That matches old behavior only if the previous handler also guarded on `.length`; if it unconditionally joined and set the header, this changes an empty-valued header into an absent header. Worth confirming against the original handler code.
